tagline: Gentle curves link coffee farms and reused buildings above Kona.
intro: Māmalahoa Kona Heritage Corridor follows two lanes with gentle curves along the slopes of Hualālai, passing coffee farms and Hōlualoa village. The road runs at 1,400 to 1,500 feet, and the Hawaiʻi Tourism Authority highlights views of Kailua-Kona and the Pacific Ocean. It also points to historic architecture, shrines and galleries along the ten-mile corridor. The route became Hawaiʻi’s first state scenic byway in March 2009.

The longer Māmalahoa Highway developed from a Hawaiian footpath encircling the island. The modern heritage corridor occupies a segment of County Route 180 inland of Kailua-Kona. Pūlama ia Kona organized a local byway committee to pursue preservation funding. A 2009 federal grant was awarded to support planning to preserve the road’s Hawaiian heritage and the history of European and Asian settlement. The grant was intended to fund a corridor management plan, bringing an inventory of historic resources into decisions about preservation and travelers’ experience of the road.

From Palani Junction, head south on Route 180 through Hōlualoa toward Honalo. The village’s former post office and telephone headquarters give way farther south to Donkey Mill, built to process coffee and now used for art. The corridor ends where Route 180 meets Route 11, Kuakini Highway.

moments.title: Hōlualoa
moments.text: Hōlualoa’s former post office once spent a night in the middle of the road. When it was moved closer to the village center, the Ueda Trucking vehicle could not finish the crossing; the move was completed the following morning. The Imin Center has a different connection to the village’s past. The county-owned Imin Center occupies the former site of Hōlualoa’s Japanese Language School, built and maintained by Japanese immigrants independently of religious organizations. Elsewhere in the village, the Immaculate Conception church is a replacement: its earlier frame building burned in December 1943 and was rebuilt within eight months.

moments.title: Kona Telephone Company building
moments.text: Telephone lines crossed Kona’s lava flows with help from mules. German immigrant Luther Aungst chose Hōlualoa as headquarters for the Kona Telephone Company, established in the 1890s. The animals dragged poles for a line running from Hilo to Kaʻū, across Kona and on to North Kohala.

moments.title: Donkey Mill Art Center
moments.text: Donkey Mill began with coffee farmers trying to make a living as prices fell. They formed the Kona Coffee Cooperative and built the mill in 1954 to process their crop. The mill now serves as an art center whose mission embraces people of all ages and abilities.
